newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat rejects Netanyahu plea to change deal.
newsitem.headline: Arafat rejects Netanyahu plea to change deal.

text.p: PLO officials said on Monday that U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross had yet to bridge wide gaps between Israel and the Palestinians on implementation of a long- delayed Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

They said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat rejected a proposal by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that they could hold a summit on Monday if Arafat agreed to change the Hebron deal signed a year ago by Israel's previous government and give Israel powers in areas that were to be given the PLO.
The Israeli prime minister told reporters at parliament: "We are in a very sensitive stage of negotiations."

Netanyahu, facing rancour in the Arab world focused on delays on implementing deals with the PLO among other things, dispatched President Ezer Weizman to Egypt on Monday in a bid to mend a deep rift at the heart of the Middle East conflict.

Chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters: "They want powers in H1. This is impossible. President Arafat's instructions are not to reopen the agreement." "H1" is the area to be handed to Palestinian rule under the signed deal.

A PLO official speaking on condition he not be identified said Arafat, in the West Bank town of Nablus, had rejected the Netanyahu proposal brought by Ross on Sunday night. Arafat left Nablus on Monday for Jordan to meet with King Hussein.
Palestinian officials say Israel is demanding security and civilian changes in the agreement.
The sides on Sunday delayed for at least one day formal talks on Hebron, set to reconvene on Monday in the Egyptian resort of Taba, to see if other channels might bear fruit.
PLO and Israeli officials said negotiators converged on some security issues, but there was no final agreement.

A PLO official said Palestinians "rejected an Israeli proposal to deploy their army on hills overlooking the heart of Hebron where some Jews live, but we did not object to another Israeli suggestion."

"Their suggestion was to deploy joint mobile units on the hills, and this isn't a problem for us because we would have overall security control of the hills and it doesn't change the agreement," the official, insisting on anonymity, said.

The ridges overlook the area of Hebron where most of some 400 Jewish settlers living amidst 100,000 Palestinians stay in fortified enclaves. According to the Hebron deal, the PLO would have immediate sole responsibility for the ridges but joint patrols could be deployed later "in parts of Hebron".

"The Palestinian Authority is fully prepared to intensify its security cooperation with Israel to put an end to Jewish extremist groups against our people in Hebron and to prevent any Palestinian group seeking to destroy the peace process," PLO security official Mohammed Dahlan said.

Other PLO officials said stumbling blocks in the talks were Israel's demand to have the right to enter PLO-controlled areas in "hot pursuit" of wanted Palestinians, rejected by Arafat, and to retain planning and zoning authorities, also ruled out.

Israeli spokesman Moshe Fogel said "there has been progress in the talks and there's greater understanding between the two sides on relative issues, but this doesn't mean there's agreement on all issues".
Western diplomats said both sides were trying to close a deal on implementation of the Hebron agreement before American elections on November 5.
